I have a old furnace in my house, approaching 20+ years now. I've fixed it a few times. Usually first by looking at parts and seeing what "doesn't look right", then looking at the symptoms online and seeing what matches. Then I watch a bunch of videos and read websites until I am fairly confident that I understand how that component works. For example, do you know what a pressure switch does, and if so, would it malfunctioning cause the symptoms you saw? Do you know what short cables could mean (probably disconnecting during vibration) and does it explain the symptoms.

Then see if you can fix it with basic tools and tape. If it fails again, order the parts online and replace the whole pathway.

Don't cheap out when ordering parts online. Manufacturer and match it perfectly. Remember, the money you save by doing it yourself far outweighs the difference in price between "cheap replacement" and "good replacement".

If it still keeps failing, move on to the next component that may have failed.

Lastly don't kill yourself. Turn off power to your furnace, and maybe even gas (don't worry furnaces self ignite, power first, then gas). Wait a few minutes for things to cool down and discharge. Take your time. Don't force things unless you are okay replacing them.

The paint on the inside of the door was wore away, and I could see a little wear on the switch itself where it pushes against it. I super glued a penny to where the switch touches the door. Problem solved.

About your inducer motor, if there was an intermittent connection for a decent amount of time and a lot of arcing, it could be damaged. It could last you another 20 years, or die to tomorrow. Most things like that are not meant to take constant surges of electricity, they are meant to take momentary surges and then keep running. Surges create a condition where it's off/on/off/on... With that said, the motor itself should be able to handle this to a decent degree.

What I would be more concerned about is the arcing that you were shown. The terminals could not be in the best of shape due to that and that might absolutely need to be cleaned or replaced. The inducer motor tends to be the most expensive part to replace in an HVAC.

Don't be afraid to troubleshoot these problems on your own.
